overview.text: Nāgas are serpent beings found across South Asian religious traditions, including Hinduism. They may be represented as snakes or as humanlike figures with cobra hoods, and art often connects them with water, fertility, and dangerous natural power. In Hindu imagery, Shesha, also called Ananta, supports the reclining Vishnu on the cosmic ocean. Another named serpent, Vasuki, serves as the rope around Mount Mandara when gods and asuras churn the Ocean of Milk for amrita, the nectar of immortality. Garuda, Vishnu’s birdlike mount, is a traditional adversary of serpents. Together the stories show that nāgas can be revered as protective or life-giving beings and feared as powerful serpents.

key_facts.text: Nāgas are serpent deities associated with water and agricultural abundance.
Some nāga figures have human bodies and cobra hoods.
Shesha, or Ananta, is the serpent on whom Vishnu reclines.
Vasuki is used as a rope in the churning of the Ocean of Milk.
Garuda, Vishnu’s birdlike mount, is depicted battling serpents.

overview.text: The four canonical Gospels are the New Testament books traditionally named Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. “Gospel” means good news, and these books tell Christian accounts of Jesus’s life, teaching, death, and resurrection. Matthew, Mark, and Luke are called Synoptic Gospels because they share many episodes and can be compared side by side; John differs more in content and style. Matthew includes the Sermon on the Mount and its Beatitudes, Luke opens with an address to Theophilus, and John narrates the wedding at Cana. Many scholars think Mark was written first, but the exact literary relationships and authorship of the books remain debated.

key_facts.text: The canonical Gospels are Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.
“Gospel” means “good news.”
Matthew, Mark, and Luke are the Synoptic Gospels.
Matthew 5 contains the Beatitudes within the Sermon on the Mount.
John 2 tells of Jesus turning water into wine at Cana.
Luke’s opening addresses Theophilus.

overview.text: In Hesiod’s Greek myth, Zeus orders the creation of Pandora after Prometheus steals fire for humans. Hephaestus shapes her from earth and water, while other gods give her abilities and adornments; her name is explained as “all endowed.” Pandora is sent to Epimetheus, who accepts her despite Prometheus’s warning against gifts from Zeus. When she opens a large jar, suffering and illness spread among people; Hope alone remains inside when the lid is shut. The familiar phrase “Pandora’s box” changes the vessel in Hesiod’s account: it is a jar. Later tellings differ about what the jar held and how to understand the remaining Hope.

key_facts.text: Hesiod presents Pandora as the first woman fashioned at Zeus’s command.
Hephaestus forms her from earth and water; Athena, Aphrodite, and Hermes contribute gifts.
Prometheus warns Epimetheus against accepting Zeus’s gift, but Epimetheus does so.
The vessel opened in Hesiod’s account is a jar, not a box.
Hope remains in the jar after its other contents escape.
Other ancient versions describe the jar and its contents differently.

overview.text: Lois Lowry’s The Giver follows twelve-year-old Jonas in a community built around order, assigned roles, and the removal of differences. At the Ceremony of Twelve, he is selected to train as Receiver of Memory, learning from the older man known as the Giver. Transmitted memories expose Jonas to color, pain, love, and experiences hidden from his neighbors. As he understands the cost of the community’s apparent safety, he questions its rules and eventually flees with the child Gabriel. The novel invites readers to weigh security against choice and emotional depth. It won the 1994 Newbery Medal and begins Lowry’s four-book Giver Quartet.

key_facts.text: Lois Lowry wrote The Giver.
Jonas is twelve when selected as the new Receiver of Memory.
The community’s strict rules erase differences, including color, pain, and love.
Jonas receives memories from the older Receiver called the Giver.
The Giver won the 1994 Newbery Medal.
Jonas escapes with Gabriel near the novel’s end.

overview.text: Weaving makes cloth by interlacing two sets of threads: lengthwise warp threads and crosswise weft threads. A loom holds the warp while a weaver passes the weft over and under it, creating a fabric whose structure and pattern depend on thread choices and technique. In Ghana and neighboring regions, Asante and Ewe artists weave narrow strips that are joined into kente cloth. Some kente patterns combine visible warp stripes with geometric weft designs, and prestige cloths have been worn for important occasions. Weaving is also a familiar mythological clue: in Hesiod’s account of Pandora, Athena teaches the newly made woman to weave.

key_facts.text: Warp threads run lengthwise; weft threads cross them.
A loom holds warp threads in place as the weft is woven through.
Kente cloth is made from narrow woven strips sewn together.
Asante and Ewe communities have traditions of kente weaving.
Kente designs can combine warp stripes and weft patterns.
Hesiod says Athena taught Pandora weaving.

overview.text: The Ten Commandments, also called the Decalogue or “Ten Words,” are a set of commands in the Hebrew Bible associated with the covenant between God and Israel. Exodus presents them at Mount Sinai after the exodus from Egypt, and Deuteronomy repeats them with some differences. They include commands concerning worship, honoring parents, Sabbath observance, murder, adultery, theft, false witness, and coveting. In the biblical narrative Moses breaks the first stone tablets after encountering worship of a golden calf; new tablets are later made. Jewish and Christian traditions study the commandments, but divide the unnumbered biblical statements into ten in different ways.

key_facts.text: The commandments appear in Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5.
The biblical setting is God’s covenant with Israel at Mount Sinai.
They prohibit murder, adultery, theft, and false witness.
Exodus 32 says Moses breaks the first tablets after seeing the golden calf.
The biblical lists are not numbered one through ten, so traditions group them differently.

overview.text: Pragmatism is a philosophical tradition that grew in the United States around thinkers Charles Sanders Peirce, William James, and John Dewey. Peirce’s pragmatic maxim asks what practical effects a concept would have; considering those effects helps clarify its meaning. James made the approach widely known through lectures collected as Pragmatism: A New Name for Some Old Ways of Thinking, including a story about a man circling a tree to see a squirrel. Dewey extended pragmatic inquiry into education, democracy, and problem solving. Pragmatists often stress experience and revisable beliefs, but they differ on questions such as truth. “Practical” here means consequences for inquiry and action, not merely what feels convenient.

key_facts.text: Charles Sanders Peirce formulated the pragmatic maxim.
William James helped popularize pragmatism.
John Dewey is another major classical pragmatist.
The maxim clarifies ideas through their conceivable practical effects.
Pragmatism treats inquiry and belief as open to revision.
James’s book Pragmatism uses a man-and-squirrel example.

overview.text: Democracy means political rule by the people, either through direct decisions or through elected representatives. Ancient Athens developed an influential direct democracy: eligible citizens could speak and vote in the assembly, while a council of 500 handled much public business. Cleisthenes’ reforms around 508 BCE reorganized citizens into new tribes and weakened inherited aristocratic ties. Athenian participation was sharply limited: women, enslaved people, and resident foreigners lacked political rights. Eligible citizens were adult men, including men without great wealth. Representative democracy uses elected people to make decisions on citizens’ behalf; this helps distinguish the Athenian assembly from many modern systems.

key_facts.text: Democracy comes from Greek words for “people” and “rule.”
Athens used an assembly in which eligible citizens could speak and vote directly.
Its council, the boulē, had 500 members chosen by lot.
Cleisthenes reorganized the citizen body into ten tribes around 508 BCE.
Women, enslaved people, and resident foreigners were excluded from Athenian politics.
Political eligibility was based on citizenship, not wealth alone.

overview.text: Alexander Pope was an English poet and satirist of the early eighteenth century, celebrated for his sharp wit and mastery of heroic couplets: pairs of rhymed lines in iambic pentameter. His mock epic The Rape of the Lock inflates a fashionable dispute over a stolen lock of Belinda’s hair into the style of grand heroic poetry. An Essay on Criticism examines writing and judgment and contains the well-known warning that a little learning is dangerous. Pope also wrote The Dunciad and produced an Iliad translation and led a collaborative Odyssey translation. A Catholic in Protestant Britain, he faced limits on formal education and public office, yet earned a living through his writing and subscriptions.

key_facts.text: Pope lived from 1688 to 1744.
He was a leading poet of the Augustan or Neoclassical age.
The Rape of the Lock is a mock epic about the cutting of Belinda’s hair.
An Essay on Criticism appeared in 1711.
Pope translated the Iliad and led a collaborative translation of the Odyssey.
His verse often uses heroic couplets.

overview.text: Andy Warhol made Marilyn Diptych in 1962, shortly after Marilyn Monroe’s death. Across two canvases he repeated the same publicity photograph from her 1953 film Niagara fifty times using silkscreen printing. Twenty-five brightly colored faces fill one panel; twenty-five black-and-white impressions fill the other, where the image becomes uneven and faint. The two-part format gives the work its name: a diptych is an artwork made of two joined panels. Warhol’s repetition evokes mass-produced images of celebrities, while the fading prints invite reflection on fame and mortality. It is a key work of Pop Art, a movement that drew subjects and methods from popular and commercial culture.

key_facts.text: Marilyn Diptych was made by Andy Warhol in 1962.
The work repeats Monroe’s face fifty times across two panels.
Its source photograph was a publicity image for Niagara (1953).
The left panel is brightly colored; the right uses fading black and white.
Warhol used silkscreen printing to repeat the image.
“Diptych” denotes a two-panel work.
